abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: A 41-year-old man with high-grade B-cell lymphoma developed neurolymphomatosis (NL) after frontline chemotherapy. He received CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy (lisocabtagene maraleucel) and subsequently developed tumor inflammation-associated neurotoxicity (TIAN) type 2, a localized neurological event distinct from immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome. Conservative treatment resulted in a neurological recovery and complete remission. This case suggests that CD19 CAR T-cell therapy may be effective for NL, and it highlights the importance of recognizing TIAN in patients with central nervous system involvement. As CAR T-cell use has increased in Japan, awareness of such complications is crucial for performing safe and effective treatment.

sec.p: Keywords: neurolymphomatosis, chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, tumor inflammation-associated neurotoxicity, high-grade B-cell lymphoma
Received 2025 Jun 5; Accepted 2025 Aug 11; Issue date 2026 May 1.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy has revolutionized the treatment of relapsed/refractory large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL) by demonstrating impressive safety and efficacy (1-3). CAR-T cell therapy may provide durable remission in a subset of patients (4,5). In addition to cytokine release syndrome (CRS), immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) (6) and tumor inflammation-associated neurotoxicity (TIAN), a distinct neurological adverse event characterized by localized neurotoxicity, has been reported in patients with central nervous system (CNS) involvement following CAR-T therapy (7). TIAN may represent a clinically distinct and symptomatic subtype of pseudo-progression. While pseudoprogression generally refers to a transient imaging worsening due to treatment-related inflammation, TIAN is distinguished by focal neurological symptoms and elevated inflammatory markers such as interleukin-6 (IL-6) in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). TIAN can be categorized into two subtypes: type 1, which is associated with inflammatory edema leading to increased intracranial pressure and potentially life-threatening herniation; and type 2, which primarily causes electrophysiological dysfunction in specific neural regions and generally results in transient exacerbation of pre-existing neurological symptoms that can be managed conservatively (7).

Neurolymphomatosis (NL) is characterized by the direct invasion of hematological malignancies, such as non-Hodgkin lymphoma (8,9), including high-grade B-cell lymphoma (HGBL) (10), into the peripheral or cranial nerves. NL may present as an initial symptom at diagnosis or may emerge secondarily during its clinical course and may manifest as painful peripheral neuropathy, radiculopathy, cranial neuropathy, and mononeuropathy multiplex (8,9). NL remains difficult to diagnose owing to its variable presentation and challenges in imaging and pathology (10). Fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography/computed tomography (FDG-PET/CT) is highly sensitive for NL (11). Recent studies have highlighted the promising efficacy of CD19 CAR-T therapy in relapsed/refractory lymphoma, including cases with primary or secondary CNS involvement (5,12), through immune surveillance using persistent CAR-T cells (13). Furthermore, CD19 CAR-T therapy has been reported to be effective and well-tolerated in NL (14).

We herein report the rare case of a patient with high-grade B-cell lymphoma (HGBL) who developed NL and subsequently became refractory to high-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX) and cytarabine. Given the anticipated poor prognosis with conventional therapy, the patient underwent CAR-T therapy, during which TIAN developed, ultimately leading to disease remission.

sec.title: Case Report
sec.p: A 41-year-old man presented with a one-month history of a right inguinal mass. On physical examination, palpable right axillary and right inguinal lymph nodes were detected, and hepatosplenomegaly was absent. Laboratory findings revealed elevated lactate dehydrogenase (346 U/L) and soluble interleukin-2 receptor (sIL-2R, 2,047 U/mL) levels. An inguinal lymph node biopsy showed a diffuse infiltrate of intermediate-sized lymphocytes with a high proliferation rate (Ki67 index of 95%), large nuclei with fine chromatin, and prominent nucleoli, thus suggesting a centroblastic morphology. An immunohistochemical analysis revealed that the abnormal lymphocytes expressed CD10, CD20, CD79a, BCL-2, BCL-6, and MUM-1 but were negative for CD3 and MYC (Fig. 1). A cytogenetic analysis demonstrated t(3;14)(q27;q32) and deletion of 6q, with fluorescence in situ hybridization confirming BCL-6 rearrangement (28%) without evidence of t(14;18) BCL2/IgH translocation or MYC rearrangement. Bone marrow aspiration revealed normocellular marrow with 3.6% abnormal lymphocyte invasion, and similar cytogenetic findings were noted. FDG-PET/CT revealed an increased uptake in the systemic lymph nodes, with a notable enlargement of the right axillary and right inguinal lymph nodes. At the initial diagnosis, no abnormal FDG uptake was observed in the cauda equina. A diagnosis of HGBL, not otherwise specified (HGBL, NOS), was made. A CSF analysis and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were not performed.

caption.p: Immunohistological findings in the right axillary lymph nodes. Intermediate-sized lymphocytes with a high proliferation rate (Ki67 index of 95%), large nuclei, fine chromatin, and prominent nucleoli were observed. The abnormal lymphocytes expressed CD10, CD20, CD79a, BCL-2, BCL-6 and MUM-1, while were negative for c-MYC. Original magnification, ×200. H&E: Hematoxylin and Eosin staining

sec.p: The patient underwent rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP) therapy, which resulted in a marked reduction in superficial lymphadenopathy. This was followed by six cycles of dose-adjusted etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and rituximab and two cycles of HD-MTX for CNS prophylaxis. Although post-treatment FDG-PET/CT showed the resolution of most lesions, an abnormal uptake was observed in the cauda equina. MRI confirmed abnormal high-intensity signals in the cauda equina (Fig. 2A). Concurrently, the patient developed left abducens nerve palsy and left facial nerve palsy. A CSF analysis demonstrated the presence of abnormal lymphocytes (Fig. 3A) that expressed CD19 with lambda light-chain restriction (Fig. 3B), establishing a diagnosis of NL. Given the primary refractory nature of HGBL, the decision was made to proceed with CD19 CAR-T therapy using lisocabtagene maraleucel (Liso-cel). A sufficient number of lymphocytes were successfully collected via apheresis.

caption.p: Longitudinal sagittal images of fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging [gadolinium (Gd)-enhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted imaging and T2-weighted imaging] at relapse (A) and post-high dose methotrexate and cytarabine (HD-MTX/Ara-C) (B).

Cytology showed abnormal lymphocytes in cerebrospinal fluid (May-Giemsa staining)(A). Original magnification, ×1,000. A flow cytometric analysis of abnormal lymphocytes. CD19/lambda light chain-positive cells were detected (B).

sec.p: Bridging chemotherapy was initiated with MTX (3.5 g/m2) and cytarabine (2 g/m2 twice daily). Additionally, intrathecal injections comprising MTX, cytarabine, and dexamethasone were administered. Despite three cycles of chemotherapy, a recurrence of the left abducens and facial nerve palsies was observed. Although head MRI revealed no gross lesions, the possibility of neural infiltration prompted the administration of whole-brain irradiation (23.4 Gy/13 fractions), which resulted in improvement of the abducens nerve palsy, while the facial nerve palsy persisted. There was sensory dullness distal to the right knee joint and left ankle joint, decreased muscle strength in the lower limbs (standing was possible with the aid of a handrail), a residual sensation of urine, and difficulty perceiving the urge to defecate. CT of the torso revealed no lesions; however, lumbar MRI demonstrated resolution of the cauda equina lesion (Fig. 2B) along with the enlargement of the right L5 nerve root (Fig. 4A).

caption.p: Longitudinal images of fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging [gadolinium (Gd)-enhanced T2-weighted imaging] of the L5 nerve root. From top to bottom: coronal, sagittal, and axial views at day -30 (A), day +16 (B), and day +34 relative to lisocabtagene maraleucel administration.

sec.p: He was transferred to our hospital (Hiroshima Red Cross Hospital and Atomic-bomb Survivors Hospital), and Liso-cel was administered following lymphodepletion with fludarabine (30 mg/m2 on days -4 to -2) and cyclophosphamide (300 mg/m2 on days -4 to -2). On day -1, the residual sensation in the urine worsened. On day +3, the patient developed grade 1 CRS accompanied by transient low back pain and constipation. On day +5, persistent fever necessitated two doses of tocilizumab. However, as the fever persisted at 39°C on day +6, with no response to the third dose of tocilizumab, tachycardia and a marked decline in the performance status were observed. Therefore, dexamethasone 10 mg was administered, thus leading to a resolution of fever by day +10 (Fig. 5).

caption.p: Clinical course of the patient. MRI: magnetic resonance imaging, CMV: cytomegalovirus

sec.p: On day +4, the patient experienced significant neurological deterioration. On day +6, the patient was unable to stand, and on day +7, muscle strength in the lower limbs decreased to Manual Muscle Testing (MMT), 2/2. On day +8, the patient developed urinary retention that required intermittent catheterization. The patient was referred to a neurologist and was diagnosed with cauda equina syndrome. A CSF analysis performed on day +8 revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis (total cell count, 102 /μL with 28% reactive lymphocytes), elevated protein (127 mg/dL), and increased IL-6 levels (244 pg/mL, reference range ＜5 pg/mL, serum IL-6 level of 36.7 pg/mL). Normal glucose (66 mg/dL) and sIL-2R (167 U/mL) levels suggested a non-infectious inflammatory process. A cytological analysis of CSF revealed an increase in atypical lymphocytes, granular lymphocytes, and basophils (Fig. 6A). Many lymphocytes were medium to large in size with a range of cytological abnormalities, including large nuclei with mildly to markedly irregular nuclear contours, mature chromatin, and scant to moderate amounts of basophilic cytoplasm (Fig. 6A). Flow cytometry failed to detect CD19-positive, lambda-restricted lymphoma cells, while CD4+ or CD8+ T-cells were observed (Fig. 6B). No pathogens [Escherichia coli, Haemophilus influenzae, Listeria, Meningococcus, Group B Streptococcus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, cytomegalovirus (CMV), Enterovirus, Herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, human herpesvirus 6, Parechovirus, Varicella-zoster virus, and Cryptococcus] that could cause meningitis were detected. Atypical lymphocytes were also observed in the peripheral blood, and mild CMV antigenemia was observed, which resolved spontaneously without treatment. These findings are consistent with those for TIAN type 2 (Fig. 5). ICANS typically presents with diffuse encephalopathy-like symptoms, whereas our patient had focal motor and bladder-rectal dysfunction corresponding to the CNS lesion, consistent with TIAN. Accordingly, a conservative management approach with close observation was adopted (corticosteroid administration was avoided to preserve the efficacy of CAR-T therapy). MRI on day +16 confirmed that the abnormal cauda equina enhancement had resolved, whereas the enlargement of the right L5 nerve root persisted (Fig. 4B). Through continuous rehabilitation, the patient's neurological function gradually improved by day +30, while intermittent catheterization was still required. His muscle strength recovered to MMT score (4/4), enabling ambulation with a walker. The patient was discharged on day +39 with an improved urinary function and mobility. Training in self-catheterization was initiated, and follow-up MRI on day +34 showed sustained resolution of the cauda equina enhancement, and the lesions in the thoracic spinal cord and L5 nerve root were also resolved (Fig. 4C). FDG-PET/CT on day +55 revealed no evidence of lymphoma recurrence. The patient regained urinary sensation and was able to void voluntarily; ambulation at home was possible with orthotic support. On MRI at day 155, the right L5 nerve root lesion regressed further. The patient was now able to walk 5-10 m without the aid of a cane. In addition, the right facial nerve palsy was observed to have nearly completely resolved.

caption.p: Cytology on day +6 showed atypical lymphocytes, granular lymphocytes and basophils in cerebrospinal fluid (May-Giemsa staining) (A). Original magnification, ×1,000. Flow cytometric analysis of lymphocytes showed the lymphocytes expressed CD3, CD4 or CD8 (B).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: We herein report a rare case of NL associated with HGBL, NOS complicated by TIAN after CD19 CAR-T therapy. This case highlights the need to recognize TIAN as a potential complication of CD19 CAR-T cell therapy, especially in patients with NL.

In the present patient, lymphoma cells were still detected in the CSF immediately prior to the initiation of lymphocyte-depleting chemotherapy for CAR-T therapy. Therefore, distinguishing type 2 TIAN from CNS lymphoma invasion is important. Owing to the atypical morphology of the cells in the CSF, a flow cytometric analysis proved useful for distinguishing lymphoma recurrence. In addition, morphological features resembling those reported for CAR-T cells were observed, thus suggesting the expansion of CAR-T cells in the CSF (15).

The patient showed localized neuropathy in the lumbar region, the initial site of lymphoma involvement. A marked elevation of the IL-6 levels in the CSF was observed, reflecting severe local inflammation. These symptoms emerged in the early days following CAR-T cell infusion, shortly after the onset of CRS, which is consistent with previously reported cases (Supplementary material). As previously suggested, the mechanism of type 2 TIAN may be associated with CRS (7). Based on the findings of the present case, CAR-T cell infiltration into NL lesions may have induced an inflammatory response, leading to worsening of NL symptoms, a process that could be described as pseudoprogression (16). More importantly, the link between type 2 TIAN and the anti-lymphoma effect warrants emphasis given the gradual improvement and eventual complete remission of NL observed in the present case.

Although TIAN may conceptually fall within the broader category of pseudoprogression, it is clinically distinct. TIAN refers to localized neurotoxicity caused by CAR-T cell infiltration into the CNS in patients with preexisting CNS involvement. Unlike typical pseudoprogression, which usually reflects tumor-related inflammation or edema, TIAN presents with focal neurological deficits temporally linked to CAR-T cell activation and often occurs without radiological tumor progression or generalized ICANS (7). Recognizing TIAN as a distinct entity is crucial for its timely and appropriate management. Recently updated data from ongoing clinical trials of anti-GD2 CAR-T therapy confirmed that TIAN is a common adverse event; however (17), it consistently resolves with a predefined toxicity management algorithm that includes intracranial pressure monitoring, neurological assessments, and interventions such as CSF drainage and administration of anakinra or corticosteroids. Notably, there have been previously reported cases in which TIAN improved without corticosteroid use, and the impact of early corticosteroid administration on TIAN outcomes remains uncertain (18).

Recently, approximately 18% of patients with CNS lymphoma treated with CD19 CAR-T therapy developed TIAN. These symptoms are typically transient and fully reversible, mirroring the clinical course observed in patients receiving GD2 CAR-T therapy. Notably, the occurrence of TIAN was associated with favorable prognosis in patients treated with CD19 CAR-T therapy (19).

Although the patient had received whole-brain radiotherapy and HD-MTX prior to CAR-T therapy, there is currently no published data demonstrating that such CNS-directed therapies increase the risk of TIAN. These interventions can disrupt the blood-brain barrier and may theoretically predispose patients to CNS inflammation (20); however, the contribution of these prior treatments to the development of TIAN in this case remains uncertain.

In our patient, the overall recovery period of 35 days was longer than that previously reported; however, the lower limb weakness resolved within approximately 10 days, consistent with previous cases. Recovery of bladder and rectal dysfunction, which is generally recognized to require more time than the improvement of limb motor deficits due to the complexity and limited resilience of the autonomic neural circuits involved, took considerably longer and likely accounted for the prolonged recovery period observed.

In a cohort of 40 biopsy-proven cases of NL, the cauda equina nerve roots were involved in 14 patients, while the lumbosacral plexus was affected in 5 patients. Following conventional therapeutic approaches, including HD-MTX and intrathecal chemotherapy, the median overall survival (mOS) for NL with secondary lymphoma was 25.4 months (9). In another large-scale retrospective analysis, the mOS was 12.0 months (10). Recently, CAR-T cell therapy has been shown to be effective against CNS lesions (21). In a study of 98 patients with secondary lymphoma involving neurological sites, including the CSF, leptomeningeal, ocular, cranial/spinal nerves, and dural/ventricular disease, CAR-T cell therapy resulted in a complete remission rate of 47%, with 37% of the patients remaining in remission at 6 months (6). Despite resistance to conventional chemotherapy, including MTX and cytarabine, our patient responded to CD19 CAR-T cell therapy, thus suggesting a potential benefit in such challenging cases.

HGBL, NOS is a newly defined aggressive B-cell lymphoma with Burkitt-like or blastoid features, which lacks double-hit cytogenetics and does not fit other subtypes. Most cases show a germinal center B cell phenotype, similar to our patient (22,23). Despite the high risk of CNS relapse, HD-MTX has not been proven effective in reducing this risk (24). Notably, our patient received HD-MTX as CNS prophylaxis; however, NL developed. HGBL, NOS is a heterogeneous disease, and a subset with a dark-zone gene signature (DZsig+) is recognized as distinct germinal center B-cell lymphoma (25). This subtype shows high BCL6 expression, high proliferation with centroblastic morphology, and elevated risk of CNS relapse (26). Although gene expression analysis was not performed, our patient's features aligned with DZsig+ lymphoma. CD3/CD20 bispecific antibodies, which are now used for relapsed/refractory lymphoblastic lymphoma, may also be effective against CNS lesions (27). Close attention should therefore be paid to adverse events similar to those associated with CAR-T cell therapy.

The favorable response in our patient suggests that CAR-T therapy may offer substantial benefits for aggressive B-cell lymphomas with NL involvement. The concept of TIAN has recently been proposed, and as such, it may have been overlooked or underdiagnosed. Hematologists should be vigilant regarding these symptoms. Early after CAR-T cell infusion, thorough examination of neurological symptoms, including a CSF analysis with flow cytometry and diagnostic imaging, is crucial to differentiate it from other complications, such as lymphoma progression and ICANS.
The patient provided written consent for publication of this report.
